Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording link: https://ff.example/recordings/ff-20250215-8347
Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Nina (Redwood SE), Leah (Redwood CSM), Carlos (Asteria CTO), Maya (Platform), Omar (SRE), Priya (Security)

Summary (auto): A technical deep dive to reconcile Asteria's strict SLOs with a hybrid hosting strategy. Focus areas: capacity planning for Dedicated vs Hosted, KV cache hot-key handling, batching and tail-latency mitigation, quantization tradeoffs for memory/latency, VPC/on-prem network implications, and fallback plans for preemptible/spot GPU usage.

Topics: capacity planning, hybrid fallback, prefix/KV cache eviction, autoscale warm pools, quantization impacts, private control plane, KMS/HSM, audit logs

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Jared: ok hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, quick roll call, and then nina will jump into the perf telemetry we pulled together
[00:00:12] Carlos: hey thanks, carlos here. we're mainly focused on the inference tail latency for patient-facing features — 95th and 99th percentiles need to be within our SLA otherwise we get paging, so that's the core constraint
[00:00:25] Nina: right, and we tuned the sample traces you sent. quick note — some names in logs got munged, so we used session ids, hope that's fine
[00:00:36] Maya: that's fine, privacy-preserving is good. can you remind us of the difference in isolation guarantees between Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted? we need to quantify noisy-neighbor risk
[00:00:48] Nina: absolutely. Dedicated provides capacity fencing — reserved GPU pools per customer with strict tenant mapping, so noisy neighbor is operationally eliminated except for infra-level failures. Hosted is multi-tenant but we use continuous capping, smart-routing and soft isolation. we also have per-tenant token-buckets and model-variant fallbacks to reduce tail impacts. the key is SLO allocation — e.g., dedicated gets pinned qps and higher priority scheduling
[00:01:11] Omar: on hosted, do you do preemption of other tenants during bursts? or do you throttle?
[00:01:18] Nina: we throttle first; if that still violates overall fairness we route lower-priority requests to cheaper variants or quantized models. for extreme bursts we have region-level burst capacity which is shared and billed extra — that's what causes noisy neighbor like behavior
[00:01:33] Carlos: ok, so for our use we think dedicated looks safer, but cost is a concern. can you show a realistic cost/latency tradeoff if we pick hybrid — some critical routes on Dedicated, others on Hosted?
[00:01:45] Jared: yes, we modeled a hybrid scenario in the spreadsheet I'll send — typical pattern we recommend: 1) critical patient-facing routes on Dedicated with warm pools sized for 95th percentile plus buffer, 2) lower-priority analytics and background processing on Hosted with autoscaling and quantized variants
[00:02:02] Nina: and add prefix caching for common prompts, that can shave a lot off the token cost and latency. prefix cache TTL and eviction are important — we'll talk about hot keys
[00:02:13] Maya: hot keys — we have a few very common system prompts. how do you prevent a single hot key from thrashing the KV cache and affecting others?
[00:02:20] Nina: we shard the KV cache per-tenant and also have hot-key detection which marks entries as "pinned" in-memory, but pinned entries consume more memory. for Dedicated you can configure larger KV cache budgets and control eviction policies. on Hosted we employ adaptive TTLs: if an item is hot it gets a slightly longer TTL but we also enforce per-key QPS limits
[00:02:38] Omar: curious about eviction policies — LRU vs LFU vs frequency-based TTL — any benchmarks?
[00:02:44] Nina: we ran a comparison on your traces: LFU with windowed decay reduced re-compute by ~18% vs pure LRU for your workload because of recurring medical templated prompts. but LFU needs more bookkeeping CPU, so tradeoff is memory+CPU vs reduced model token ops
[00:02:58] Carlos: interesting. what about batching? our traffic is spiky but with many short sequences, can batching help without blowing tail latency?
[00:03:08] Nina: continuous batching helps but it's workload dependent. we used latency-aware batching where we bound max latency per request and only batch within that window. e.g., a 10ms batching window gave 2-3x throughput improvements for your mid-sized requests with <1ms median overhead added, but tail had slight increase — we compensate by reserving a fraction of the cluster for low-latency lanes (no-batch lanes)
[00:03:28] Maya: so that warm pool idea — how do you size it? what's a conservative heuristic?
[00:03:34] Jared: start with 95th-perc concurrency observed, add 20-30% to account for growth and burst, and include a warm-up profile for cold KV cache misses. we provided a sample sizing calc in the pilot template: consider GPU startup times, model load times (particularly with larger quantized models), and prefix cache cold start costs
[00:03:52] Priya: on encryption and compliance — if we go hybrid, can we keep keys on-prem? how does integr with KMS/HSM work?
[00:03:59] Nina: yes. for Redwood Private or Dedicated in a VPC we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. keys never leave your control plane in Private — for Hosted we offer envelope encryption with BYOK options to integrate with your cloud KMS. we'll send the integration guide
[00:04:14] Priya: do audit logs include per-token traceability? we need detailed trails for compliance — who requested what model, which variant served, latency, and correlation ids
[00:04:21] Leah: logs capture per-request metadata including model_version, variant, latency, cost estimate, and user_token. retention is configurable. for Private we can ship a forwarder to your SIEM
[00:04:31] Carlos: nailed — back to fallback strategies — say we lose Dedicated capacity due to maintenance or node failure, what's the automatic behavior?
[00:04:38] Nina: multi-step: 1) automatic reroute to Hosted-compatible model variants in the same region, 2) if regional is saturated, fallback to cross-region threads with higher latency but still within a configured alert window, 3) we optionally enable degraded-mode responses (e.g., shorter generations or deterministic templates) to preserve throughput. we also support pre-warming of Hosted variants if Dedicated goes down routinely
[00:04:57] Omar: cross-region raises data residency headaches — how do we preserve residency on failover?
[00:05:02] Jared: residency constraints can be encoded in routing policies. if you mark a route as region-resident only, then we won't failover cross-region; instead we'd trigger capacity escalation to dedicated or an SLA incident and avoid violating residency. it's a configuration knob
[00:05:18] Maya: quantization — we heard 4-bit vs 8-bit tradeoffs. for our models (sequence length ~1024) what's the expected latency and accuracy cost?
[00:05:27] Nina: in our benching 4-bit (GPT-style Q4) saved ~40-50% memory and gave 1.1-1.25x latency improvement on GPU kernels, but some rare tokens had higher distributional shift. 8-bit is a safer middle ground: 20-30% memory savings, ~1.05x latency improvement, very minor quality delta. recommend A/B evals on your prompt set for critical routes
[00:05:48] Carlos: we will need a quantization regression threshold — e.g., <1% change in patient-facing answer correctness. can you hook up Redwood Optimize to monitor these regressions?
[00:05:55] Jared: yes, Redwood Optimize can run continuous evals on your golden prompt set and alert on drift beyond thresholds. we can tie alerts to rollback runbooks
[00:06:06] Maya: networking — VPC peering costs and egress might dominate if we frequently fallback cross-region. any tips?
[00:06:12] Nina: colocate Dedicated in the same cloud region/zone as your VPC to avoid egress. for cross-region fallbacks consider compressing payloads, and use shorter response strategies to reduce transfer. also pre-estimate egress based on 95th percentile bytes per response multiplied by fallback frequency in the cost model
[00:06:28] Omar: if we use spot/preemptible GPUs as part of Dedicated burst pool, how do you orchestrate replacements? preemptions can cause model load storms
[00:06:36] Nina: we treat spot as warm burst capacity only; we maintain a small hot pool of on-demand instances to absorb preemption pain. when a spot is lost, we spin up replacements while shifting traffic to the hot pool and to hosted variants. we also stagger model loads and use lazy weight loading to reduce spike memory usage during node churn
[00:06:55] Carlos: what about observability — can we get per-tenant token-level cost attribution and tail-latency breakdowns?
[00:07:01] Leah: yes — console gives per-route dashboards, token-level cost, p50/p95/p99 latency histograms, and request traces. we can attach custom tags (e.g., patient-id hashed) for correlation. we also provide a Prometheus exporter for SRE teams
[00:07:14] Maya: ok for the pilot we'd like: 1) dedicated for /patient-qna and /triage short routes, 2) hosted for analytics and async jobs, 3) optimize prefix cache and LFU settings, and 4) measure 48-hour hot-key behavior.
[00:07:25] Jared: yep, I'll share pilot template and the cost delta scenarios. Nina will run the KV sims and Leah will enable trial observability for your account
[00:07:33] Priya: final question — do you offer an on-prem private control plane that still receives Redwood-managed updates but sits behind our firewall?
[00:07:41] Nina: yes, that's Redwood Private with a customer-managed control plane; updates are signed and you can choose air-gap windows. we also support hybrid—control plane on-prem, data plane in your VPC
[00:07:52] Carlos: great, that covers it. thanks, we'll review the pilot docs and reconvene once we see the KV sim results
[00:08:00] Jared: awesome, we'll follow up. thanks all

End of recording.
